claim: The photoreceptor layer of the retina is completely avascular.
source: The completely avascular photoreceptor layer of the retina lies between the vascular inner retina (on its apical aspect) and the highly vascularized and permeable fenestrated choriocapillaris (Blaauwgeers et al., 1999) (on its basal aspect) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blaauwgeers et al., 1999 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The photoreceptor layer lies between the vascular inner retina on its apical aspect and the highly vascularized fenestrated choriocapillaris on its basal aspect.
source: The completely avascular photoreceptor layer of the retina lies between the vascular inner retina (on its apical aspect) and the highly vascularized and permeable fenestrated choriocapillaris (Blaauwgeers et al., 1999) (on its basal aspect) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blaauwgeers et al., 1999 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The choroid has the highest blood flow of any vascular bed.
source: The choroid, which has the highest flow of any vascular bed (Bill et al., 1983), fulfills the metabolic and oxygen demands of the retinal pigmental epithelium (RPE) cells and photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bill et al., 1983.

claim: The choroid fulfills the metabolic and oxygen demands of the RPE cells and photoreceptors.
source: The choroid, which has the highest flow of any vascular bed (Bill et al., 1983), fulfills the metabolic and oxygen demands of the retinal pigmental epithelium (RPE) cells and photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bill et al., 1983 and established knowledge about choroidal function.

claim: In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), angiogenic vessels from the inner retina extend into the photoreceptors, a process called retinal angiomatous proliferation (RAP).
source: In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), angiogenic vessels from the inner retina extend into the photoreceptors (retinal angiomatous proliferation, or RAP), or from choroidal vessels breaching through the complex of the RPE and Bruch's membrane (BrM) into the subretinal space (choroidal neovascularization, CNV).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about AMD pathology.

claim: In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), angiogenic vessels from choroidal vessels breach through the RPE and Bruch's membrane into the subretinal space, a process called choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
source: In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), angiogenic vessels from the inner retina extend into the photoreceptors (retinal angiomatous proliferation, or RAP), or from choroidal vessels breaching through the complex of the RPE and Bruch's membrane (BrM) into the subretinal space (choroidal neovascularization, CNV).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about AMD pathology.

claim: CNV and RAP can disrupt retinal structure and function, causing irreversible vision loss.
source: Either can disrupt retinal structure and function, causing irreversible vision loss (Ambati et al., 2003b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ambati et al., 2003b.

claim: AMD is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the West.
source: Although AMD is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the West (Ambati et al., 2003b), its etiology has not been fully elucidated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ambati et al., 2003b.

claim: The etiology of AMD has not been fully elucidated.
source: Although AMD is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the West (Ambati et al., 2003b), its etiology has not been fully elucidated.
evidence: This claim is based on the state of knowledge at the time of publication.

claim: VEGF-A is a potent angiogenic factor with a crucial role in both normal and pathologic vascular growth within the eye.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) is a potent angiogenic factor with a crucial role in both normal and pathologic vascular growth within the eye (Saint-Geniez et al., 2008; Saint-Geniez et al., 2009; Rajappa et al., 2010; Carmeliet Jain, 2011; Potente et al., 2011), and its increased expression is linked to pathologic proliferation of abnormal, highly permeable vessels into the avascular photoreceptor layers (Amin et al., 1994; Ambati et al., 2003b; Rajappa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Saint-Geniez et al., 2008; Saint-Geniez et al., 2009; Rajappa et al., 2010; Carmeliet Jain, 2011; Potente et al., 2011.

claim: Increased expression of VEGF-A is linked to pathologic proliferation of abnormal, highly permeable vessels into the avascular photoreceptor layers.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) is a potent angiogenic factor with a crucial role in both normal and pathologic vascular growth within the eye (Saint-Geniez et al., 2008; Saint-Geniez et al., 2009; Rajappa et al., 2010; Carmeliet Jain, 2011; Potente et al., 2011), and its increased expression is linked to pathologic proliferation of abnormal, highly permeable vessels into the avascular photoreceptor layers (Amin et al., 1994; Ambati et al., 2003b; Rajappa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 1994; Ambati et al., 2003b; Rajappa et al., 2010.

claim: sFLT-1 (sVEGFR-1) is a soluble isoform of VEGF receptor-1.
source: A soluble isoform of VEGF receptor-1 (sVEGFR-1, also known as sFLT-1) acts as a naturally occurring inhibitor of VEGF-A-mediated angiogenesis (Kendall and Thomas, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kendall and Thomas, 1993.

claim: sFLT-1 acts as a naturally occurring inhibitor of VEGF-A-mediated angiogenesis.
source: A soluble isoform of VEGF receptor-1 (sVEGFR-1, also known as sFLT-1) acts as a naturally occurring inhibitor of VEGF-A-mediated angiogenesis (Kendall and Thomas, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kendall and Thomas, 1993.

claim: sFLT-1 negatively regulates VEGF-A action by binding and sequestering VEGF-A.
source: sFLT-1 negatively regulates VEGF-A action: first, it binds and sequesters VEGF-A; and second, by heterodimerizing with membrane-bound VEGF-receptor-2, it prevents VEGF-A occupancy and subsequent signal transduction (Kendall et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kendall et al., 1996.

claim: sFLT-1 negatively regulates VEGF-A action by heterodimerizing with membrane-bound VEGF-receptor-2, preventing VEGF-A occupancy and subsequent signal transduction.
source: sFLT-1 negatively regulates VEGF-A action: first, it binds and sequesters VEGF-A; and second, by heterodimerizing with membrane-bound VEGF-receptor-2, it prevents VEGF-A occupancy and subsequent signal transduction (Kendall et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kendall et al., 1996.

claim: Excess levels of sFLT-1 strongly inhibit CNV in mice and monkeys.
source: Excess levels of sFLT-1 strongly inhibit CNV in mice and monkeys (Lai et al., 2005; Lukason et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lai et al., 2005 and Lukason et al., 2011.

claim: Endogenous sFLT-1 is both necessary and sufficient for corneal avascularity.
source: In addition, we previously demonstrated that endogenous sFLT-1 is both necessary and sufficient for corneal avascularity (Ambati et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ambati et al., 2006.

claim: Soluble FLT-1 expression was significantly decreased in the RPE and photoreceptor layers in all AMD eyes compared with age-matched controls.
source: Both results demonstrated that soluble FLT-1 was strikingly decreased in the RPE and photoreceptor layers in all AMD (n = 3) and RAP eyes (n = 3) compared with age matched controls, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Soluble FLT-1 expression was significantly decreased in the RPE and photoreceptor layers in all RAP eyes compared with age-matched controls.
source: Both results demonstrated that soluble FLT-1 was strikingly decreased in the RPE and photoreceptor layers in all AMD (n = 3) and RAP eyes (n = 3) compared with age matched controls, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: VEGF-A was upregulated significantly in the retina of AMD eyes.
source: conversely, as has been previously reported, VEGF-A was upregulated significantly in the retina of AMD eyes (Ambati et al., 2003b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ambati et al., 2003b.

claim: In situ hybridization and immunostaining confirmed the presence of sFLT-1 mRNA and protein, respectively, in photoreceptors and RPE.
source: In situ hybridization and immunostaining confirmed the presence of sFLT-1 mRNA and protein, respectively, in photoreceptors and RPE, which indicated that both cell types can synthesize and express sFLT-1 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Both photoreceptors and RPE can synthesize and express sFLT-1.
source: In situ hybridization and immunostaining confirmed the presence of sFLT-1 mRNA and protein, respectively, in photoreceptors and RPE, which indicated that both cell types can synthesize and express sFLT-1 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of both mRNA and protein in these cell types, as shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The relative expression pattern of soluble FLT-1 to VEGF is higher in the photoreceptors than in the inner vascular layers of the retina.
source: Compared with VEGF-A (Figure 1C), the relative expression pattern of soluble FLT-1 to VEGF is higher in the photoreceptors than in the inner vascular layers of the retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VEGF is prominent in the inner vascularized retina, the layer which harbors blood vessels and neurons.
source: A theoretical implication is that VEGF is prominent in the inner vascularized retina, the layer which harbors blood vessels and neurons, while sFLT-1 is prominent in the outer avascular retina, consistent with our initial hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression pattern data and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: sFLT-1 is prominent in the outer avascular retina.
source: A theoretical implication is that VEGF is prominent in the inner vascularized retina, the layer which harbors blood vessels and neurons, while sFLT-1 is prominent in the outer avascular retina, consistent with our initial hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression pattern data and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: sFLT-1 was principally detected on the basal aspect of the RPE–BrM complex, facing the vascularized choroid.
source: Furthermore, sFLT-1 was principally detected on the basal aspect of the RPE–BrM complex, facing the vascularized choroid (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: In the RPE, VEGF-A localizes on both basal and apical surfaces.
source: In contrast, in the RPE, VEGF-A localizes on both basal and apical surfaces, consistent with a prior report (Blaauwgeers et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blaauwgeers et al., 1999.

claim: The polarized distribution of sFLT-1 in the RPE is reminiscent of sFLT-1 expression in the cornea, where the highest levels of sFLT-1 are found in the perilimbal region counterposing the vascularized conjunctiva.
source: This polarized distribution is reminiscent of sFLT-1 expression in the cornea, where the highest levels of sFLT-1 are found in the perilimbal region counterposing the vascularized conjunctiva (Ambati et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ambati et al., 2007.

claim: VEGF has a vasculotrophic role in the choroid.
source: This is consistent with VEGF's vasculotrophic role in the choroid and neurotrophic role in the photoreceptors (Saint-Geniez et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saint-Geniez et al., 2008.

claim: VEGF has a neurotrophic role in the photoreceptors.
source: This is consistent with VEGF's vasculotrophic role in the choroid and neurotrophic role in the photoreceptors (Saint-Geniez et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saint-Geniez et al., 2008.

claim: Subretinal injection of a neutralizing antibody against FLT-1 in wild type mice resulted in increased free VEGF-A levels.
source: First, we injected a neutralizing antibody against FLT-1 into the subretinal space in wild type mice. This resulted in increased free VEGF-A levels (n = 10; p<0.005) and induced CNV (n = 10, p<0.00005; Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Subretinal injection of a neutralizing antibody against FLT-1 in wild type mice induced CNV.
source: First, we injected a neutralizing antibody against FLT-1 into the subretinal space in wild type mice. This resulted in increased free VEGF-A levels (n = 10; p<0.005) and induced CNV (n = 10, p<0.00005; Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by FA and OCT data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sequestration of VEGF-A by FLT-1 maintains subretinal avascularity.
source: This resulted in increased free VEGF-A levels (n = 10; p<0.005) and induced CNV (n = 10, p<0.00005; Figure 2A,B), suggesting that sequestration of VEGF-A by FLT-1 maintains subretinal avascularity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that blocking FLT-1 increases VEGF-A and induces CNV.

claim: Subretinal injection of FLT-1 neutralizing antibody in Flt-1 tk−/− mice induced CNV accompanied with higher VEGF levels.
source: Next, we administered FLT-1 neutralizing antibody (which occupies domains 1–4 of this receptor) via subretinal injection in Flt-1 tk−/− mice, which are deficient in the tyrosine kinase domain of membrane-bound FLT-1 (Hiratsuka et al., 1998). The results demonstrated that the induced CNV in Flt-1 tk−/− mice was accompanied with higher VEGF levels (n = 10; p<0.005; Figure 2C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and imaging data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: CNV occurs due to disruption of sFLT-1, but not of mFLT-1 activity.
source: The results demonstrated that the induced CNV in Flt-1 tk−/− mice was accompanied with higher VEGF levels (n = 10; p<0.005; Figure 2C,D), strongly suggesting that CNV occurs due to disruption of sFLT-1, but not of mFLT-1 activity (which is inactive in these mice).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results in Flt-1 tk−/− mice, which lack functional membrane-bound FLT-1.

claim: Soluble but not membrane-bound FLT-1 plays a key role in anti-angiogenic regulation.
source: This accords with prior studies which have found that soluble but not membrane-bound FLT-1 plays a key role in anti-angiogenic regulation, based on the finding that germline Flt-1 deletion leads to embryonic lethality due to vascular endothelial hyperplasia, while membrane-bound Flt-1 lacking the tyrosine kinase domain is sufficient for normal vascular development in mice (Fong et al., 1995; Kappas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fong et al., 1995 and Kappas et al., 2008.

claim: Germline Flt-1 deletion leads to embryonic lethality due to vascular endothelial hyperplasia.
source: This accords with prior studies which have found that soluble but not membrane-bound FLT-1 plays a key role in anti-angiogenic regulation, based on the finding that germline Flt-1 deletion leads to embryonic lethality due to vascular endothelial hyperplasia, while membrane-bound Flt-1 lacking the tyrosine kinase domain is sufficient for normal vascular development in mice (Fong et al., 1995; Kappas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fong et al., 1995 and Kappas et al., 2008.

claim: Membrane-bound Flt-1 lacking the tyrosine kinase domain is sufficient for normal vascular development in mice.
source: This accords with prior studies which have found that soluble but not membrane-bound FLT-1 plays a key role in anti-angiogenic regulation, based on the finding that germline Flt-1 deletion leads to embryonic lethality due to vascular endothelial hyperplasia, while membrane-bound Flt-1 lacking the tyrosine kinase domain is sufficient for normal vascular development in mice (Fong et al., 1995; Kappas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fong et al., 1995 and Kappas et al., 2008.

claim: Subretinal injections of FLT-1 neutralizing antibody and isotype control in wild type mice showed no significant difference in PlGF expression at day 3.
source: To determine if PlGF is essential for CNV, we performed subretinal injections of anti-FLT-1 and isotype control antibody in wild type mice and found no significant difference in PlGF expression between both groups at day 3 (n = 9; Figure 2E) or at day 10 (undetectable levels).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PlGF levels were undetectable at day 10 after subretinal injections of FLT-1 neutralizing antibody and isotype control in wild type mice.
source: To determine if PlGF is essential for CNV, we performed subretinal injections of anti-FLT-1 and isotype control antibody in wild type mice and found no significant difference in PlGF expression between both groups at day 3 (n = 9; Figure 2E) or at day 10 (undetectable levels).
evidence: This claim is based on ELISA measurements.

claim: CNV induced by FLT-1 blockade is mediated by desequestration of VEGF-A, not of PlGF or VEGF-B.
source: Taken together with the above finding that FLT-1 antibody induced CNV in Flt-1 tk−/− mice (in which VEGF-B signaling would be expected to be inoperative), this indicates that CNV induced by FLT-1 blockade is mediated by desequestration of VEGF-A, not of PlGF or VEGF-B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results in Flt-1 tk−/− mice and PlGF measurements.

claim: Neither PlGF nor VEGF-B are able to compensate for VEGF-A during its blockade.
source: Moreover, neither PlGF nor VEGF-B are able to compensate for VEGF-A during its blockade, and mice lacking either factor display only minor developmental defects (Malik et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malik et al., 2006 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Mice lacking PlGF display only minor developmental defects.
source: Moreover, neither PlGF nor VEGF-B are able to compensate for VEGF-A during its blockade, and mice lacking either factor display only minor developmental defects (Malik et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malik et al., 2006 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Mice lacking VEGF-B display only minor developmental defects.
source: Moreover, neither PlGF nor VEGF-B are able to compensate for VEGF-A during its blockade, and mice lacking either factor display only minor developmental defects (Malik et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malik et al., 2006 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: In contrast to VEGF-A, VEGF-B is neither induced by hypoxia nor essential to angiogenesis.
source: Furthermore, it is well established that, in contrast to VEGF-A, VEGF-B is neither induced by hypoxia nor essential to angiogenesis (Hoeben et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoeben et al., 2004 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: VEGF-B is critical for blood vessel survival in pathological conditions.
source: Although VEGF-B is dispensable for blood vessel growth, it is critical for blood vessel survival in pathological conditions (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The neutralizing anti-FLT-1 antibody did not significantly affect ELISA readings of VEGF-A.
source: The presence of anti-FLT-1 antibody did not significantly affect ELISA readings of either cytokine.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The neutralizing anti-FLT-1 antibody did not significantly affect ELISA readings of PlGF-2.
source: The presence of anti-FLT-1 antibody did not significantly affect ELISA readings of either cytokine.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Recombinant FLT-1 abolished detection of VEGF-A over background levels, indicating that VEGF-A bound to FLT-1 is not detected by the ELISA assay.
source: Recombinant FLT-1 was added to each concentration of VEGF-A (A) or PlGF-2 (B) and abolished detection of VEGF-A and PlGF-2 over background levels, indicating that VEGF-A or PlGF-2 that is bound to FLT-1 is not detected by this assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Recombinant FLT-1 abolished detection of PlGF-2 over background levels, indicating that PlGF-2 bound to FLT-1 is not detected by the ELISA assay.
source: Recombinant FLT-1 was added to each concentration of VEGF-A (A) or PlGF-2 (B) and abolished detection of VEGF-A and PlGF-2 over background levels, indicating that VEGF-A or PlGF-2 that is bound to FLT-1 is not detected by this assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: FLT-1 neutralizing antibody released VEGF-A but not PlGF-2 from recombinant FLT-1.
source: Finally, we determined whether anti-FLT-1 neutralizing antibody released VEGF-A but not PlGF-2 from recombinant FLT-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). After coating ELISA plates with FLT-1 and then incubating with VEGF-A or PlGF-2, Flt-1 neutralizing antibody was added. The results demonstrate that FLT-1 neutralizing antibody released VEGF-A but not PlGF-2 from recombinant FLT-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Subretinal delivery of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp demonstrated efficient transduction of the RPE and the photoreceptor layer.
source: Subretinal delivery of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp demonstrated efficient transduction of the RPE and the photoreceptor layer (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp resulted in downregulation of sFLT-1 compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp resulted in downregulation of sFLT-1 (Figure 3A), increased free VEGF-A (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B), and induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp resulted in increased free VEGF-A compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp resulted in downregulation of sFLT-1 (Figure 3A), increased free VEGF-A (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B), and induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp induced CNV compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, treatment with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp resulted in downregulation of sFLT-1 (Figure 3A), increased free VEGF-A (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B), and induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.05; Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by FA, OCT, and histology data shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 induced primary CNV as well as secondary CNV 4 weeks after injection.
source: Furthermore, as we reported recently (Luo et al., 2013), AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 induced primary CNV (defined as a CNV that initially occurred at the injection site), as well as secondary CNV (defined as a lesion that is more than ½ a disc diameter from the primary CNV lesion, and that shows no leakage on fluorescein angiography (FA) at least 2 weeks after injection) 4 weeks after injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2013.

claim: Secondary CNV was not found in the controls, although insignificant CNV developed initially due to injury.
source: This phenomenon was not found in the controls, although insignificant CNV developed initially due to injury.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from control experiments.

claim: Subretinal delivery of pCre in Vegfalox/lox mice reduced VEGF protein in RPE cells.
source: The reduction of VEGF protein in RPE cells via subretinal delivery of a plasmid encoding Cre recombinase (pCre) in Vegfaloxp/loxp mice was demonstrated by immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Increased VEGF-A expression in the RPE/choroid and CNV in Vegfalox/lox mice treated with subretinal AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 was suppressed by subretinal delivery of pCre.
source: Increased VEGF-A expression in the RPE/choroid (n = 10; p<0.0005) and CNV (n = 10; p<0.05) in Vegfalox/lox mice treated with subretinal AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 (Figure 3D) was suppressed by subretinal delivery of pCre.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The release of sequestered VEGF-A is requisite for CNV development following sFLT-1 antagonism.
source: This confirms that the release of sequestered VEGF-A is requisite for CNV development following sFLT-1 antagonism.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that CNV induced by sFLT-1 knockdown is suppressed when VEGF-A is also reduced.

claim: AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp and AAV.shRNA.Gfp up-regulated IFN-γ compared with AAV.Gfp and PBS in C57BL/6J mice.
source: We found that AAV.shRNA, targeting either sFlt-1 or a non-specific sequence, up-regulated IFN-γ (n = 10; p<0.01) and IL-12 (n = 10; p<0.001; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6), both of which are induced by TLR3.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp and AAV.shRNA.Gfp up-regulated IL-12 compared with AAV.Gfp and PBS in C57BL/6J mice.
source: We found that AAV.shRNA, targeting either sFlt-1 or a non-specific sequence, up-regulated IFN-γ (n = 10; p<0.01) and IL-12 (n = 10; p<0.001; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6), both of which are induced by TLR3.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: IFN-γ and IL-12 are induced by TLR3.
source: We found that AAV.shRNA, targeting either sFlt-1 or a non-specific sequence, up-regulated IFN-γ (n = 10; p<0.01) and IL-12 (n = 10; p<0.001; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6), both of which are induced by TLR3.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about TLR3 signaling.

claim: Non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp failed to induce CNV in wild type mice.
source: However, non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp failed to induce CNV in wild type mice (n = 10; Figure 3B), suggesting that CNV formation in AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp treated mice is due not to non-specific immune activation but rather to sFLT-1 suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CNV formation in AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp treated mice is due to sFLT-1 suppression rather than non-specific immune activation.
source: However, non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp failed to induce CNV in wild type mice (n = 10; Figure 3B), suggesting that CNV formation in AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp treated mice is due not to non-specific immune activation but rather to sFLT-1 suppression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that non-specific shRNA does not induce CNV despite immune activation.

claim: Subretinal injection of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp but not non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp increased VEGF-A levels in Tlr3–/– mice.
source: Subretinal injection of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp (n = 10) but not non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp (n = 10) increased VEGF-A levels (p<0.05) and induced CNV (p<0.005) in Tlr3–/– mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Subretinal injection of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp but not non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp induced CNV in Tlr3–/– mice.
source: Subretinal injection of AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp (n = 10) but not non-specific AAV.shRNA.Gfp (n = 10) increased VEGF-A levels (p<0.05) and induced CNV (p<0.005) in Tlr3–/– mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FA and ELISA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Levels of IFN-γ and IL-12 were not significantly different in Tlr3–/– mice treated with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.Gfp or AAV.shRNA.Gfp.
source: Levels of IFN-γ and IL-12 were not significantly different in either group (n = 10; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6), suggesting that CNV is due to sFLT-1 knockdown rather than non-specific immune activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: CNV in Tlr3–/– mice is due to sFLT-1 knockdown rather than non-specific immune activation.
source: Levels of IFN-γ and IL-12 were not significantly different in either group (n = 10; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6), suggesting that CNV is due to sFLT-1 knockdown rather than non-specific immune activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results in Tlr3–/– mice showing CNV without immune activation.

claim: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice reduced sFLT-1.
source: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice reduced sFLT-1, induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.01), and increased free VEGF-A in the RPE/choroid (n = 8; p<0.01) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice induced CNV.
source: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice reduced sFLT-1, induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.01), and increased free VEGF-A in the RPE/choroid (n = 8; p<0.01) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice increased free VEGF-A in the RPE/choroid.
source: Subretinal injection of pCre in Flt-1lox/lox mice reduced sFLT-1, induced CNV (n = 10; p<0.01), and increased free VEGF-A in the RPE/choroid (n = 8; p<0.01) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cre expression in Vmd2-cre+ mice is restricted to the RPE.
source: The results showed that Cre expression, as indicated by tomato deletion resulting in exclusive Egfp fluorescence, was restricted to the RPE in floxed mT/mG mice bred with Vmd2-cre+ and to the photoreceptors in floxed mT/mG mice crossed with the iCre-75+ line (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cre expression in iCre-75+ mice is restricted to the photoreceptors.
source: The results showed that Cre expression, as indicated by tomato deletion resulting in exclusive Egfp fluorescence, was restricted to the RPE in floxed mT/mG mice bred with Vmd2-cre+ and to the photoreceptors in floxed mT/mG mice crossed with the iCre-75+ line (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 82% of homozygous RPE-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/lox) developed CNV.
source: At 1–3 months of age, nearly all homozygous RPE-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/lox) (18/22 eyes, 82%; p<0.001), and about half of the heterozygous conditional Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/+) (17/42 eyes, 40%; p=0.009) developed CNV, which progressed over time, compared with 18% (2/22 eyes, 9%) of littermate controls (Vmd2-cre+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 40% of heterozygous RPE-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/+) developed CNV.
source: At 1–3 months of age, nearly all homozygous RPE-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/lox) (18/22 eyes, 82%; p<0.001), and about half of the heterozygous conditional Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/+) (17/42 eyes, 40%; p=0.009) developed CNV, which progressed over time, compared with 18% (2/22 eyes, 9%) of littermate controls (Vmd2-cre+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 9% of littermate controls (Vmd2-cre+flt-1+/+) developed CNV.
source: At 1–3 months of age, nearly all homozygous RPE-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/lox) (18/22 eyes, 82%; p<0.001), and about half of the heterozygous conditional Flt-1 knockout mice (Vmd2-cre+flt-1lox/+) (17/42 eyes, 40%; p=0.009) developed CNV, which progressed over time, compared with 18% (2/22 eyes, 9%) of littermate controls (Vmd2-cre+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 57% of homozygous photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (iCre-75+flt-1lox/lox) developed RAP.
source: Similarly, at 1–3 months of age, both homozygous (iCre-75+flt-1lox/lox, 8/14 eyes, 57%; p<0.05) and heterozygous (13/24 eyes, 54%; p<0.05) photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (iCre-75+flt-1lox/+) developed RAP, compared with 10% (1/10 eyes) of littermate controls (iCre-75+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 54% of heterozygous photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (iCre-75+flt-1lox/+) developed RAP.
source: Similarly, at 1–3 months of age, both homozygous (iCre-75+flt-1lox/lox, 8/14 eyes, 57%; p<0.05) and heterozygous (13/24 eyes, 54%; p<0.05) photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (iCre-75+flt-1lox/+) developed RAP, compared with 10% (1/10 eyes) of littermate controls (iCre-75+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: At 1–3 months of age, 10% of littermate controls (iCre-75+flt-1+/+) developed RAP.
source: Similarly, at 1–3 months of age, both homozygous (iCre-75+flt-1lox/lox, 8/14 eyes, 57%; p<0.05) and heterozygous (13/24 eyes, 54%; p<0.05) photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice (iCre-75+flt-1lox/+) developed RAP, compared with 10% (1/10 eyes) of littermate controls (iCre-75+flt-1+/+).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: The number of lesions with leakages on FA ranged from one to four per eye in the floxed animals.
source: The number of lesions with leakages on FA ranged from one to four per eye in the floxed animals, whereas in littermate controls, there was no more than one neovascular lesion per eye.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from FA imaging.

claim: In littermate controls, there was no more than one neovascular lesion per eye.
source: The number of lesions with leakages on FA ranged from one to four per eye in the floxed animals, whereas in littermate controls, there was no more than one neovascular lesion per eye.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from FA imaging.

claim: RAP lesions started from the inner retina (arising from retinal vessels) at an early stage and invaded the photoreceptor layer, eventually anastomosing with the choroidal neovasculature.
source: RAP lesions started from the inner retina (arising from retinal vessels) at an early stage and invaded the photoreceptor layer, eventually anastomosing with the choroidal neovasculature (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5 and Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and histology data shown in Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5.

claim: Rare CNV occurrences in littermate controls may be accounted for by Cre 'leakiness' or toxicity.
source: We observed rare CNV occurrences in the littermate controls. These results may be accounted for by Cre 'leakiness' or toxicity, which has been reported in several transgenic models using the Cre-lox system (Editorial, 2007; Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Editorial, 2007 and Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007.

claim: Cre 'leakiness' or toxicity has been reported in several transgenic models using the Cre-lox system.
source: We observed rare CNV occurrences in the littermate controls. These results may be accounted for by Cre 'leakiness' or toxicity, which has been reported in several transgenic models using the Cre-lox system (Editorial, 2007; Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Editorial, 2007 and Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007.

claim: sFLT-1 was down-regulated in the conditional Flt-1 knockout mice compared with littermate controls.
source: We further confirmed that sFLT-1 was down-regulated by in situ hybridization and IHC, while VEGF-A was up-regulated by western blotting in the conditional Flt-1 knockout mice, compared with littermate controls (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 6)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and IHC data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: VEGF-A was up-regulated in the conditional Flt-1 knockout mice compared with littermate controls.
source: We further confirmed that sFLT-1 was down-regulated by in situ hybridization and IHC, while VEGF-A was up-regulated by western blotting in the conditional Flt-1 knockout mice, compared with littermate controls (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 6)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: CNV/RAP occurrence in conditional Flt-1 knockout mice is due to sFLT-1 knockdown in the RPE or photoreceptors.
source: We further confirmed that sFLT-1 was down-regulated by in situ hybridization and IHC, while VEGF-A was up-regulated by western blotting in the conditional Flt-1 knockout mice, compared with littermate controls (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 6), suggesting CNV/RAP occurrence is due to sFLT-1 knockdown in the RPE or photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between sFLT-1 knockdown and CNV/RAP development.

claim: No changes in sFLT-1 expression were observed in the inner retinae of the two conditional Flt-1 knockouts.
source: We observed no changes in sFLT-1 expression in the inner retinae of the two conditional Flt-1 knockouts.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from IHC staining.

claim: sFLT-1 expression was somewhat decreased in the inner retina following subretinal injection with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1.
source: However, sFLT-1 expression was somewhat decreased in the inner retina following subretinal injection with AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1. This may be due to diffusion and leakage of the injection fluid along the injection track.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: No CNV lesions were seen on retinal sections of VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice at p7, p14, and p21.
source: To determine whether the CNV/RAP lesions we observed were due to preceding retinal changes, we performed IHC staining on sections of VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice at p7, p14, and p21. No CNV lesions were seen on retinal sections at these timepoints.
evidence: This claim is based on IHC staining data.

claim: Evidence of nascent choroidal endothelial changes abutting Bruch's membrane was found at p21 in VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice.
source: However, we found evidence of nascent choroidal endothelial changes abutting Bruch's membrane at p21 (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: No CNV was observed on FA at p21 in VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice.
source: At p21, the earliest feasible timepoint for angiography, we observed no CNV on FA (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by FA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: The earliest timepoint that CNV was detected angiographically in VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice was at p28.
source: The earliest timepoint that we detected CNV angiographically was at p28 (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by FA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: Early choroidal vascular changes occur without changes in the overlying neural retina in VMD-Crefltloxp/loxp mice.
source: Taken together, these data indicate early choroidal vascular changes without changes in the overlying neural retina.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal sequence of observations showing choroidal changes before neural retinal changes.

claim: ADAM10 is the only described protease that cleaves membrane-bound FLT-1 to the soluble isoform.
source: To the best of our knowledge, ADAM10 is the only described protease that cleaves membrane-bound FLT-1 to the soluble isoform (Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: ADAM10 is expressed in the inner retinal layers but not in the RPE or photoreceptors.
source: We found that ADAM10 is expressed in the inner retinal layers (Figure 5), but not in the RPE or photoreceptors where we found that knockdown of sFLT-1 breached photoreceptor avascular privilege.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A proteolytic cleavage-mediated origin for outer retinal sFLT-1 is unlikely.
source: Hence, a proteolytic cleavage-mediated origin for outer retinal sFLT-1 is unlikely.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of ADAM10 expression in the RPE and photoreceptors.

claim: The neovascular processes observed in RPE/photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice recapitulate many of the characteristics of human CNV or RAP.
source: The neovascular processes we observed, either of CNV or RAP phenotypes in RPE/photoreceptor-specific Flt-1 knockout mice, recapitulate many of the characteristics of human CNV or RAP (different subtypes of AMD) (Donati et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Donati et al., 2006.

claim: The mouse models presented exhibit CNV or RAP in heterozygous transgenic mice within a rapid timeframe.
source: In contrast to the transgenic mice which develop CNV in senility (Ambati et al., 2003a; Imamura et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2011) or a model of RAP in the systemic VLDLR−/− mouse (Heckenlively et al., 2003), the mouse models presented herein exhibit CNV or RAP in heterozygous transgenic mice as well and within a rapid timeframe, indicating the vital role of sFLT-1 in maintaining the integrity of photoreceptor avascular privilege.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from the transgenic mouse models and supported by citations to Ambati et al., 2003a; Imamura et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2011; Heckenlively et al., 2003.

claim: sFLT-1 plays a vital role in maintaining the integrity of photoreceptor avascular privilege.
source: In contrast to the transgenic mice which develop CNV in senility (Ambati et al., 2003a; Imamura et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2011) or a model of RAP in the systemic VLDLR−/− mouse (Heckenlively et al., 2003), the mouse models presented herein exhibit CNV or RAP in heterozygous transgenic mice as well and within a rapid timeframe, indicating the vital role of sFLT-1 in maintaining the integrity of photoreceptor avascular privilege.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rapid development of CNV/RAP in sFLT-1 knockout mice.

claim: Transgenic mice which overexpress VEGF-A in either RPE or photoreceptors developed intrachoroidal neovascularization or retinal neovascularization but not CNV or RAP.
source: Moreover, previous studies found that transgenic mice which overexpress VEGF-A in either RPE or photoreceptors developed intrachoroidal neovascularization or retinal neovascularization but not CNV or RAP (Okamoto et al., 1997; Schwesinger et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okamoto et al., 1997 and Schwesinger et al., 2001.

claim: Overexpression of VEGF-A in the retina or RPE is not sufficient to overcome the subretinal vascular barrier to induce CNV.
source: These phenomena suggest that overexpression of VEGF-A in the retina or RPE is not sufficient to overcome the subretinal vascular barrier to induce CNV.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VEGF-A overexpression alone does not induce CNV.

claim: Mice with reduced sFLT-1 expression in the RPE developed CNV, indicating that sFLT-1 down-regulation is sufficient to cause CNV.
source: On the other hand, in our study, mice with reduced sFLT-1 expression in the RPE developed CNV, indicating that sFLT-1 down-regulation is sufficient to cause CNV.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from the conditional knockout mice.

claim: The ratio of soluble FLT-1 to VEGF is likely critical to the maintenance of the subretinal vascular barrier.
source: Hence, the ratio of soluble FLT-1 to VEGF is likely critical to the maintenance of the subretinal vascular barrier.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that both VEGF overexpression alone and sFLT-1 reduction alone have different effects.

claim: The transgenic models presented more closely mimic human AMD than previous models.
source: Further, the models presented herein more closely mimic human AMD, rendering these transgenic models quite useful for further studies and translational applications.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous models and the characteristics of the new models.

claim: Less CNV was observed in the injection site after AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 delivery than after antibody or genomic knockdown.
source: We observed less CNV in the injection site after AAV.shRNA.sFlt-1 delivery than after antibody or genomic knockdown; this may be due to persistence of preformed sFLT-1, as the turnover of this protein in the RPE is, to our knowledge, unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Lower levels of both VEGF-A and CNV were observed in Vegfalox/lox mice compared with wild type mice in AAV-mediated sFlt-1 knockdown studies.
source: Another interesting observation is that lower levels of both VEGF-A and CNV were observed in Vegfalox/lox mice compared with wild type mice in AAV-mediated sFlt-1 knockdown studies.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data from the experiments.

claim: The insertion of lox sites flanking the VEGF-A gene can affect gene expression in conditions of injury.
source: It is possible that the insertion of lox sites flanking the VEGF-A gene can affect gene expression in conditions of injury. This could be due to several mechanisms including disruption of cis-regulatory elements, interruption of unknown miRNA binding sites, and effects on mRNA stability by the palindromic nature of loxp sites. Loxp insertion has previously been reported to affect the transcription of genes in cis in selected circumstances (Sun and Storb, 2001; Meier et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Sun and Storb, 2001 and Meier et al., 2010.

claim: Protein blockade, transcriptional silencing, or genomic ablation of sFLT-1 can induce CNV/RAP.
source: Nonetheless, taken together, our findings demonstrate that protein blockade, transcriptional silencing, or genomic ablation of sFLT-1 can induce CNV/RAP, showing that sFLT-1, through sequestration of VEGF-A, is a key molecular defender of vision-critical photoreceptor avascular privilege.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined results from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: sFLT-1, through sequestration of VEGF-A, is a key molecular defender of vision-critical photoreceptor avascular privilege.
source: Nonetheless, taken together, our findings demonstrate that protein blockade, transcriptional silencing, or genomic ablation of sFLT-1 can induce CNV/RAP, showing that sFLT-1, through sequestration of VEGF-A, is a key molecular defender of vision-critical photoreceptor avascular privilege.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that sFLT-1 suppression leads to CNV/RAP.

claim: Reduced VEGF-A expression has been observed in CNV specimens surgically obtained from patients with persistent CNV not responsive to anti-VEGF-A therapy.
source: Reduced VEGF-A expression has been observed in CNV specimens surgically obtained from patients with persistent CNV not responsive to anti-VEGF-A therapy. This reduction may explain why some patients stop responding to anti-VEGF-A therapy after a period of time (Tatar et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tatar et al., 2009.

claim: Endothelial sFLT-1 expression is regulated by VEGF.
source: Endothelial sFLT-1 expression is regulated by VEGF, acts as an autocrine regulator of endothelial cell function, and controls angiogenesis (Ahmad et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmad et al., 2011.

claim: Endothelial sFLT-1 acts as an autocrine regulator of endothelial cell function.
source: Endothelial sFLT-1 expression is regulated by VEGF, acts as an autocrine regulator of endothelial cell function, and controls angiogenesis (Ahmad et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmad et al., 2011.

claim: Endothelial sFLT-1 controls angiogenesis.
source: Endothelial sFLT-1 expression is regulated by VEGF, acts as an autocrine regulator of endothelial cell function, and controls angiogenesis (Ahmad et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmad et al., 2011.

claim: Some endogenous angiogenesis inhibitors (e.g., pigment epithelium-derived factor) in the RPE/Bruch's membrane/choriocapillaris complex have been reported to be reduced in AMD.
source: Some endogenous angiogenesis inhibitors (e.g., pigment epithelium-derived factor) in the RPE/Bruch's membrane/choriocapillaris complex have been reported to be reduced in AMD and may contribute to the barrier against choroidal neovascular invasion (Bhutto et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bhutto et al., 2008.

claim: Reduced endogenous angiogenesis inhibitors may contribute to the barrier against choroidal neovascular invasion in AMD.
source: Some endogenous angiogenesis inhibitors (e.g., pigment epithelium-derived factor) in the RPE/Bruch's membrane/choriocapillaris complex have been reported to be reduced in AMD and may contribute to the barrier against choroidal neovascular invasion (Bhutto et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Bhutto et al., 2008.

claim: The findings offer greater insight into the molecular mechanisms responsible for retinal vascular demarcations and CNV/RAP.
source: Nevertheless, the findings in this study offer greater insight into the molecular mechanisms responsible for retinal vascular demarcations and CNV/RAP, and the described molecular advances have broader ramifications.
evidence: This claim is based on the overall interpretation of the study results.

claim: The findings impact testing of anti-angiogenic pharmaceuticals.
source: They impact testing of anti-angiogenic pharmaceuticals, may illuminate the mechanistic basis of angiogenesis in other diseases affecting over a billion people (Potente et al., 2011), hold translational import for a key cause of blindness, and support the ongoing clinical trial of AAV.sFlt-1 for the treatment of neovascular AMD (clinical trial NCT01024998 at www.clinicaltrials.gov).
evidence: This claim is speculative about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: The findings may illuminate the mechanistic basis of angiogenesis in other diseases affecting over a billion people.
source: They impact testing of anti-angiogenic pharmaceuticals, may illuminate the mechanistic basis of angiogenesis in other diseases affecting over a billion people (Potente et al., 2011), hold translational import for a key cause of blindness, and support the ongoing clinical trial of AAV.sFlt-1 for the treatment of neovascular AMD (clinical trial NCT01024998 at www.clinicaltrials.gov).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Potente et al., 2011.

claim: The findings support the ongoing clinical trial of AAV.sFlt-1 for the treatment of neovascular AMD.
source: They impact testing of anti-angiogenic pharmaceuticals, may illuminate the mechanistic basis of angiogenesis in other diseases affecting over a billion people (Potente et al., 2011), hold translational import for a key cause of blindness, and support the ongoing clinical trial of AAV.sFlt-1 for the treatment of neovascular AMD (clinical trial NCT01024998 at www.clinicaltrials.gov).
evidence: This claim is based on the relevance of the findings to the clinical trial.

claim: The findings highlight a potential use of sFLT-1 as a therapeutic target in situations where angiogenesis is desirable.
source: Further, they highlight a potential use of sFLT-1 as a therapeutic target in situations where angiogenesis is desirable, as well as a new role for sFLT-1, which has recently been found to protect renal podocytes (Jin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: sFLT-1 has recently been found to protect renal podocytes.
source: Further, they highlight a potential use of sFLT-1 as a therapeutic target in situations where angiogenesis is desirable, as well as a new role for sFLT-1, which has recently been found to protect renal podocytes (Jin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2012.

claim: The genetic models of AMD described are the first which exhibit CNV or RAP spontaneously at an early age.
source: and the genetic models of AMD we describe are the first which exhibit CNV or RAP spontaneously at an early age, rendering them original non-invasive platform technologies with a variety of applications.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous models.
